about.title: National City Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: National City property owners, from small businesses along National City Boulevard to apartment complexes near E Plaza Boulevard, have a legal duty to keep their premises reasonably safe. When they fail to fix a known hazard, like a wet floor, broken stair, or poorly lit parking lot, and someone gets hurt, California law allows the injured person to pursue compensation. These claims hinge on proving the owner knew or reasonably should have known about the danger and did nothing about it. That's why what happens in the hours after a fall matters so much: photos of the hazard, witness names, and any available surveillance footage can make or break a claim. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves, but we can connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney in our network who understands how San Diego County premises cases are built and can evaluate what you're dealing with.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a National City Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Had Notice
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew, or should have known, about the hazard and failed to address it. An attorney can help identify maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records that establish this.

items.title: Acting Before the Two-Year Clock Runs
items.desc: Most premises claims must be filed within two years, but if a government-owned property is involved, such as a public sidewalk near I-5, the window can be much shorter. Getting an evaluation early protects your options.

items.title: Comparative Fault Won't Automatically Sink Your Claim
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, meaning you can still recover compensation even if you were partly responsible for the fall, though your share of fault can reduce the amount recovered.

items.question: I fell in a store on National City Boulevard but didn't report it right away. Can I still pursue a claim?
items.answer: You may still have a valid claim, but delays can make it harder to preserve evidence like surveillance video, which many businesses only retain for a limited time. It's worth having an independent attorney review your situation as soon as possible. Documentation from your medical visit and any witnesses can also help support your case.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for not seeing the hazard?
items.answer: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover compensation even if you share some responsibility for the fall. Your total recovery would simply be reduced by your percentage of fault. An attorney can help assess how fault might be allocated in your specific case.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in National City?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the injury to file a lawsuit against a private property owner. If the fall happened on public property, like a city sidewalk or municipal building, the deadline is often much shorter and requires an early formal claim. Because these timelines vary, it's best to get an evaluation soon after the incident.
